sections.title: OOP in Java, C++, Python and C#

blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site as of November 2026 for a computer science student, in the style of the other guides. Examples use Java, with Python and C++ where the languages differ. Worked numbers were checked by program. Where a vendor, a standard or a language version matters, check the official source before relying on a detail.

The ideas are the same everywhere; the **defaults and the machinery** differ. Many interview questions ("why does Java not have multiple inheritance?", "what is a virtual destructor?") are really questions about those differences.

| Feature | Java | C++ | Python | C# |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Typing | static, compiled to bytecode | static, compiled to machine code | **dynamic**, interpreted | static, compiled to IL |
| Memory management | **garbage collector** | **manual** (RAII, smart pointers) | garbage collector (reference counting + cycle detector) | garbage collector |
| Multiple class inheritance | **no** (interfaces only) | **yes** (virtual inheritance for the diamond) | **yes** (MRO) | no (interfaces only) |
| Method overriding by default | **every instance method is virtual** | only if declared `virtual` | every method can be replaced | only with `virtual` / `override` |
| Constructors / destructors | constructors; no destructor (use try-with-resources) | constructors **and destructors** | `__init__`; `__del__` rarely used | constructors; finalisers; `IDisposable` |
| Access control | `private`, package, `protected`, `public` | `private`, `protected`, `public` | **by convention** (`_x`, `__x` name mangling) | like Java, plus `internal` |
| Interfaces | `interface` | abstract class with pure virtual functions | abstract base classes, protocols (duck typing) | `interface` |
| Generics | **type erasure** | **templates** (instantiated per type) | not needed (dynamic) | reified generics |
| Operator overloading | no (except `+` on String) | **yes** | **yes** (dunder methods) | yes |
| Everything is an object | no (primitives exist) | no | **yes** (even ints and functions) | no |
| Parameter passing | by value (references are values) | by value, by reference (`&`), by pointer | object references (like Java) | by value, `ref`, `out` |

- Java: single class inheritance + interfaces, GC, all instance methods virtual.
- C++: multiple inheritance, manual memory, `virtual` is opt-in, destructors, templates.
- Python: duck typing, dunder methods, no real `private`, multiple inheritance with the MRO.
- C#: Java-like, plus properties, delegates and events, `struct` value types.
- Java generics are erased at run time; C++ templates generate code per type.
blocks.title: One-line differences that get asked
Key points
blocks.text:
- Java: GC, single inheritance, virtual by default
- C++: manual memory, destructors, multiple inheritance, virtual is opt-in
- Python: dynamic typing, duck typing, convention-based privacy, MRO for multiple inheritance
- Generics: Java erases them, C++ instantiates templates

The C++ code in this chapter is standard C++17 written to be short and was checked by reading, not compiled here. Compile it yourself with `g++ -std=c++17 file.cpp` to see the output. The Python and Java snippets were run.
blocks.title: About the C++ snippets

blocks.text:
### C++: the object lifetime is yours

In C++ objects can live on the **stack** (destroyed automatically at the end of the scope) or the **heap** (`new`, destroyed with `delete`). Because there is no garbage collector, a class releases its resources in its **destructor**, and the idiom **RAII** (resource acquisition is initialisation) ties a resource (memory, file, lock) to an object's lifetime: the resource is acquired in the constructor and released in the destructor, even when an exception is thrown. Modern C++ uses `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr` instead of raw `new` and `delete`.

Without `virtual` on `~Base`, deleting a `Derived` through a `Base*` is **undefined behaviour**: the `Derived` destructor would not run. A class meant to be a base class needs a virtual destructor.

**Object slicing.** Copying a `Derived` object into a variable of type `Base` (by value) copies only the `Base` part and loses the derived data and behaviour. Pass polymorphic objects by pointer or reference.

**Rule of three/five.** If a class manages a resource and needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it probably needs all three (and move operations, the rule of five). Otherwise two copies would both free the same resource: a double free. The **rule of zero** says to use members that manage themselves (`std::string`, `std::vector`, smart pointers) so you write none of them.

| C++ term | Meaning | Java counterpart |
|---|---|---|
| `virtual` function | dispatched at run time | every instance method |
| pure virtual (`= 0`) | abstract method | `abstract` method |
| class with only pure virtuals | interface | `interface` |
| copy constructor | how a copy is made | `clone()` or a copy constructor |
| reference `T&` | alias, cannot be null or reseated | none |
| `const` member function | does not modify the object | `final` fields / immutable class |

### Python: everything is dynamic

That prints `Account('Asha', 150) 150 True` and then `0.04 0.04`.

**Key Python points:**

- **Duck typing and the MRO.** There is no `implements`. For multiple inheritance Python linearises the parents with the **C3 algorithm**; `ClassName.__mro__` shows the order and `super()` follows it, which solves the diamond problem predictably.
- **No true private members.** `_x` is a hint, `__x` triggers **name mangling** (renamed to `_Class__x`), but nothing is enforced: "we are all consenting adults".
- **Dunder methods** (`__init__`, `__str__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`, `__len__`, `__iter__`, `__enter__`/`__exit__`) let your objects work with built-in syntax.
- **Mutable default arguments** are shared between calls:

blocks.code:
def add(item, bucket=[]):          # the list is created ONCE, when the function is defined
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add(1), add(2))              # [1, 2] [1, 2]  not [1] [2]

blocks.text: By convention and by tools: prefix internal names with an underscore, expose controlled access with `@property`, and validate in setters or methods. Double underscores trigger name mangling to avoid accidental clashes in subclasses, not real privacy. Python relies on programmer discipline and documentation instead of enforcement.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Python has no private keyword. How do you encapsulate?
Key points
blocks.text:
- C++: stack or heap objects, destructors, RAII, virtual destructors for base classes
- Slicing copies only the base part: pass polymorphic objects by pointer or reference
- Rule of three/five/zero: manage resources with smart pointers and standard containers
- Python: duck typing, @property, dunder methods, convention-based privacy
- Beware Python's shared mutable default arguments

**Low-level design (LLD)** interviews ask you to turn a short problem statement into classes. A reliable method:

1. **Clarify requirements** (vehicle types, floors, payment, how tickets work). Write down what is in and out of scope.
2. **Find the nouns** (candidate classes: Vehicle, ParkingSpot, ParkingLot, Ticket) and the **verbs** (candidate methods: park, unpark, calculateFee).
3. **Decide relationships:** is-a (inheritance), has-a (composition), uses (dependency).
4. **Apply principles and patterns where they pay off:** Strategy for pricing, Factory for vehicles, no pattern if none is needed.
5. **Walk through scenarios** (a car enters, the lot is full, a vehicle leaves) and handle the edge cases.

blocks.title: ParkingLot.java

blocks.text: **Design notes an interviewer will ask about.** *Why a `Strategy` for pricing?* Rates change without touching the lot (open/closed). *Why records for `Vehicle` and `Ticket`?* They are immutable values. *Where would you add concurrency?* `park` must be made atomic (a lock or a concurrent structure), otherwise two cars can take the same spot. *How would it scale?* Index free spots by size (a queue per size) instead of scanning all spots.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- LLD method: requirements, nouns and verbs, relationships, principles and patterns, scenarios
- Use enums and records for fixed sets and value objects
- Strategy keeps changeable rules (pricing) out of the core class
- State the concurrency story: make the critical operation atomic
- Say how the design would change for scale

These are the OOP questions asked most often, with the short answer that scores.

| Question | Answer in one breath |
|---|---|
| Overloading vs overriding | Overloading: same name, different parameters, chosen at compile time by declared types. Overriding: same signature in a subclass, chosen at run time by the object's class. |
| Abstract class vs interface | Abstract class: state, constructors, partial implementation, single inheritance. Interface: a contract (plus default methods), no instance state, many per class. |
| Can a constructor be overridden / inherited? | No: constructors are not inherited, so they cannot be overridden; they can be overloaded and chained with `this(...)` and `super(...)`. |
| Can a class have a private constructor? | Yes: for singletons, utility classes and factory-only construction. |
| `this` vs `super` | `this` is the current object; `super` refers to the parent part, used to call its constructor or an overridden method. |
| `final` / `finally` / `finalize` | `final`: constant, no override, no subclass. `finally`: block that always runs after try. `finalize`: deprecated pre-GC hook: do not use it. |
| Can you override a static method? | No: it is hidden. Static methods are bound to the class at compile time. |
| What is the `Object` class? | The root of every class: `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `getClass`, `clone`, `wait`, `notify`. |
| Shallow vs deep copy | Shallow copies references; deep copies the whole object graph. |
| Aggregation vs composition | Both has-a; in composition the part cannot outlive the whole. |
| Is Java 100% object-oriented? | No: it has primitives (`int`, `double`) and static members. Wrapper classes box primitives. |
| Why are Strings immutable? | Security, thread safety, string pool sharing, cached hash code, safe as map keys. |
| What does polymorphism need? | Inheritance or an interface, overriding, and a superclass reference to a subclass object. |

### Output puzzles

Work out what each program prints, then check yourself against the answers below.

blocks.title: Puzzles.java

blocks.text: Answers: **1** `A-static B-static A-init A() B-init B()` (static blocks run once when the class loads, parent first; then for each object: parent instance initialisers and constructor, then the child's). **2** `A-init A() B-init B()` (the static blocks do not run again). **3** `finally ` then `1` (the `finally` block runs before the method returns). **4** `long`: with the argument `5` (an `int`), the compiler prefers **widening** (`int` to `long`) over **boxing** (`Integer`) over the `Object` overload. **5** `true false true`: `Integer` objects between −128 and 127 are cached, so `==` happens to work for 127 but not for 128, which is why you use `equals`. **6** `a12 3a`: strings concatenate left to right, but `1 + 2` evaluated first gives 3.

Pick a real one (a `PaymentMethod` interface with card, UPI and wallet implementations, or a `Notifier` with email and SMS). Say what the interface promises, how the caller depends only on the interface, how a new implementation is added without editing the caller (open/closed), and how you tested it by passing a fake. Concrete beats textbook.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Explain a polymorphism example from your own project.
Key points
blocks.text:
- Know the one-breath answers: overloading versus overriding, abstract class versus interface, shallow versus deep copy
- Static blocks run once per class load; instance initialisers and constructors run per object
- Overload resolution prefers widening, then boxing, then varargs
- Integer caching makes == unreliable above 127: use equals
- A strong answer ties a concept to something you built

15 original questions on 10 areas. *Recall* questions test a definition or a rule. *Problem* questions give you numbers or a short scenario to work out. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people.

o: A-static B-static A() B() A() B()
A-static B-static A() B() A-static B-static A() B()
A() B() A() B() A-static B-static
items.w: Static initialisers run once, when the class is first initialised, and a parent is initialised before its child. Constructors run for every object, parent first, so the second `new B()` prints only "A() B()".
The return value 1 is computed, then the finally block runs (printing "finally "), and only then does the method return, so main prints 1 afterwards.

o: it does not compile because the call is ambiguous
items.w: The argument 5 is an int. Overload resolution tries, in order: exact match or widening primitive conversion (int to long), then boxing (Integer), then boxing with widening reference conversion (Object). The first phase finds g(long).
`Integer.valueOf` caches values from −128 to 127, so a and b are the same object. 128 is outside the cache, so c and d are two different objects, but `equals` compares the values.
Evaluation goes left to right: 1 + 2 is integer addition giving 3, then + "a" starts string concatenation ("3a"), and the remaining 1 and 2 are appended as text: "3a12".

o: a compile-time error: a non-static method cannot be called from a static context
items.w: `main` is static, so there is no `this` object. An instance method needs an object to run on, so you must write `new Main().inc()` or make the method static.

items.q:
*(Problem)* What does this program print?
```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
print(add(1), add(2))
```
items.w: The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared by every call that does not pass its own. Both calls append to the same list, and both results refer to it. Use `None` as the default and create the list inside the function.

items.q:
*(Problem)* What does this program print?
```python
class C:
    items = []
a = C()
b = C()
a.items.append(1)
print(b.items)
```
items.w: `items` is a class attribute, so a and b share the same list. Appending through `a` changes the shared object. Assigning `a.items = []` instead would create a separate instance attribute.

The method resolution order of D is D, B, C, A. `super()` in B calls the next class in D's MRO, which is C (not A), and C's `super()` then reaches A, giving "B" + "C" + "A". Each class is visited once, which solves the diamond problem.

A class that defines `__eq__` without `__hash__` gets `__hash__` set to None, so its instances are unhashable and cannot go in a set. Defining both (consistently) fixes it, just as in Java's equals and hashCode contract.
A property defined with only a getter is read-only. Assigning to it raises AttributeError, which is caught, and the stored value is unchanged.

items.q: *(Recall)* In C++, deleting an object of a derived class through a pointer to a base class whose destructor is not virtual results in
o: undefined behaviour, typically skipping the derived class's destructor
items.w: Without a virtual destructor the call is bound statically to the base destructor, so the derived part is not cleaned up properly. Classes meant to be used polymorphically need a virtual destructor.

o: a class has too many virtual functions
a derived object is copied into a base-class variable by value, losing the derived part
a pointer is cast to void*
items.w: Copying a Derived into a Base variable by value copies only the Base subobject, so the extra data and the overridden behaviour of Derived are lost. Passing by pointer or reference avoids it.

items.q: *(Recall)* A key difference between Java generics and C++ templates is that
o: Java generics can be used with primitive types directly
C++ templates are checked only at run time
Java generics are faster than templates
Java erases type arguments at run time, while C++ generates separate code for each instantiation
items.w: Java generics use type erasure: a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are the same class at run time, which is why you cannot create `new T()`. C++ templates are instantiated per type at compile time. Java generics cannot hold primitives directly (use `Integer`).

items.q: *(Recall)* At the start of a low-level design interview, the best first step is to
o: clarify the requirements and scope, then identify the main entities and actions
choose the design patterns to use
items.w: Clarifying requirements and scope prevents designing the wrong thing. Entities (nouns) and actions (verbs) then give candidate classes and methods; patterns are applied only where they solve a real problem.

blocks.text: #### OOP in Java, C++, Python and C#

items.question: Why is every instance method virtual in Java but not in C++?
items.answer: Java chose safety and simplicity: overriding always works, and the JIT removes the cost when only one implementation exists. C++ follows the principle of not paying for what you do not use, so a method is dispatched dynamically only if it is declared `virtual`.

items.question: How does Python get polymorphism without declaring interfaces?
items.answer: Through duck typing: if an object has the method the caller uses, it works ("if it walks like a duck..."). The type is checked only when the call is made at run time, so unrelated classes with the same method name are interchangeable.

blocks.text: #### C++ and Python specifics

items.question: Why must a base class intended for polymorphic use have a virtual destructor in C++?
items.answer: Deleting a derived object through a base-class pointer calls only the base destructor if it is not virtual (undefined behaviour), so derived resources are never released. A virtual destructor makes the call dispatch to the derived destructor first.

items.question: What does `__mro__` give you in Python?
items.answer: The method resolution order: the linear sequence of classes searched when looking up a method or attribute, computed with the C3 algorithm. `super()` follows it, which makes multiple inheritance and the diamond problem predictable.

blocks.text: #### Low-level design: a parking lot

items.question: What are the first things you should do in a low-level design interview?
items.answer: Clarify the requirements and scope (actors, features, constraints), then identify the main entities (nouns) and actions (verbs) before drawing classes. Starting to code immediately usually leads to a design that misses requirements.

items.question: Why is the parking lot's pricing a Strategy instead of an if/else on vehicle type inside the lot class?
items.answer: Pricing is a rule that changes independently of parking logic. Behind a Strategy interface a new pricing scheme is a new class, and the lot never changes: the open/closed principle, plus easy testing of each scheme alone.

blocks.text: #### Interview traps and answers

items.question: What happens if both the `try` block and the `finally` block contain a return statement?
items.answer: The value returned by the `finally` block overrides the one from `try` (and discards any exception), which is why returning from `finally` is considered bad practice. The compiler warns about it.

items.question: In what order do static blocks, instance initialisers and constructors run for `new B()` where B extends A?
items.answer: When class B is first used: A's static initialisers, then B's static initialisers (once only). For each new object: A's instance initialisers and A's constructor, then B's instance initialisers and B's constructor.
